sudan.title: الاقتصاد السوداني.. توقعات تتحقق والأزمة تتفاقم - سودان تربيون
sudan.summary: تواجه الاقتصاد السوداني تحديات متزايدة، حيث تتزايد الأزمات الاقتصادية والاجتماعية. تشير التوقعات إلى تفاقم الوضع، مع ارتفاع معدلات التضخم ونقص السلع الأساسية. يعاني المواطنون من صعوبة في الحصول على الغذاء والدواء، مما يزيد من الضغوط على الحكومة. كما أن الأزمات السياسية تؤثر سلبًا على الاستقرار الاقتصادي، مما يؤدي إلى تراجع الاستثمارات. في ظل هذه الظروف، يتطلع الكثيرون إلى حلول عاجلة لتحسين الوضع الاقتصادي، لكن التحديات الكبيرة لا تزال قائمة.

sudan.title: المنفي يجدد دعم ليبيا لـ«وحدة السودان» وسيادته - عين ليبيا
sudan.summary: جدد رئيس المجلس الرئاسي الليبي، محمد المنفي، دعم ليبيا لوحدة السودان وسيادته. جاء ذلك خلال لقائه مع رئيس مجلس السيادة السوداني، عبد الفتاح البرهان، حيث تم التأكيد على أهمية تعزيز العلاقات الثنائية بين البلدين. المنفي أعرب عن استعداد ليبيا للمساهمة في دعم السودان في مختلف المجالات، بما في ذلك الأمن والتنمية. كما تم مناقشة التحديات التي تواجه السودان، وأهمية التعاون الإقليمي والدولي في دعم استقرار البلاد. اللقاء يعكس التزام ليبيا بدعم الجهود الرامية إلى تحقيق السلام والاستقرار في السودان.

sudan.title: الجيش يعلن التصدي لهجوم لتحالف الدعم السريع والشعبية بالنيل الأزرق - سودان تربيون
sudan.summary: أعلن الجيش السوداني تصديه لهجوم شنته قوات الدعم السريع والحركة الشعبية في ولاية النيل الأزرق. وأكد المتحدث باسم الجيش أن القوات المسلحة تمكنت من صد الهجوم، مشيراً إلى وقوع اشتباكات عنيفة بين الطرفين. وأوضح أن الجيش يواصل عملياته العسكرية في المنطقة لضمان الأمن والاستقرار. يأتي هذا التصعيد في ظل الأوضاع المتوترة في السودان، حيث تتزايد الاشتباكات بين القوات الحكومية والمجموعات المسلحة. وقد دعا الجيش المواطنين إلى الابتعاد عن مناطق النزاع، محذراً من تداعيات هذه الاشتباكات على المدنيين.

sudan.title: مقتل وإصابة 40 شخصا جراء قصف الضعين بشرق دارفور - Radio Dabanga
sudan.summary: قُتل 40 شخصاً وأصيب آخرون جراء قصف استهدف مدينة الضعين في شرق دارفور. الهجوم، الذي وقع في وقت متأخر من الليل، أسفر عن دمار واسع في المنطقة، حيث تم تدمير العديد من المنازل والمرافق. وقد أدانت السلطات المحلية الهجوم، مشيرة إلى أنه يأتي في سياق تصاعد العنف في المنطقة. كما تم الإبلاغ عن نزوح عدد من الأسر نتيجة للاشتباكات المستمرة. يُعتبر هذا الحادث جزءاً من أزمة أوسع في دارفور، حيث تتزايد التوترات بين الجماعات المختلفة.

sudan.title: مسيرة تستهدف سوقا وتقتل 53 شخصا - Hespress
sudan.summary: مسيرة تستهدف سوقا في إحدى المناطق أسفرت عن مقتل 53 شخصا، حيث وقع الهجوم أثناء تجمع حشود كبيرة في السوق. الهجوم، الذي يُعتقد أنه عمل إرهابي، أدى إلى إصابة العديد من الأشخاص بجروح خطيرة. السلطات المحلية بدأت تحقيقات عاجلة لتحديد هوية المنفذين وتفاصيل الحادث. وقد أدان المسؤولون هذا العمل الوحشي، داعين إلى الوحدة والتضامن في مواجهة الإرهاب. كما تم الإعلان عن إجراءات أمنية مشددة في المنطقة لضمان سلامة المواطنين.

sudan.title: أنباء عن مقتل العشرات في أبيي المتنازع عليها بين السودان وجنوب السودان - الجزيرة نت
sudan.summary: أفادت تقارير عن مقتل العشرات في منطقة أبيي المتنازع عليها بين السودان وجنوب السودان، حيث اندلعت مواجهات عنيفة بين القوات المسلحة للبلدين. وتشير المعلومات الأولية إلى أن الاشتباكات أسفرت عن سقوط العديد من الضحايا، بالإضافة إلى نزوح عدد كبير من السكان المحليين. تأتي هذه الأحداث في وقت حساس، حيث يسعى المجتمع الدولي إلى تهدئة التوترات بين الجانبين. وقد دعت منظمات حقوق الإنسان إلى ضرورة اتخاذ إجراءات عاجلة لحماية المدنيين في المنطقة. الوضع في أبيي يظل متأزماً، مما يزيد من المخاوف من تصاعد العنف في المستقبل.

sudan.title: احتجاجات في ابيي واستدعاء السفير السوداني في جوبا بسبب قصف سوق النعام (أميت) الحدودي - Dabanga Radio TV Online - Radio Dabanga
sudan.summary: شهدت منطقة أبيي احتجاجات واسعة بعد قصف سوق النعام (أميت) الحدودي، مما أدى إلى استدعاء السفير السوداني في جوبا. القصف، الذي يُعتقد أنه ناتج عن توترات بين القوات السودانية والجنوبية، أسفر عن أضرار كبيرة في السوق وأثار غضب السكان المحليين. المتظاهرون طالبوا بتحقيق العدالة ومحاسبة المسؤولين عن الهجوم، كما دعوا إلى تعزيز الأمن في المنطقة. الحكومة الجنوبية أكدت أنها ستتخذ إجراءات للتحقيق في الحادث، بينما أعربت عن قلقها إزاء تصاعد التوترات على الحدود. تأتي هذه الأحداث في وقت حساس، حيث تسعى الأطراف إلى استقرار الوضع في المنطقة المتنازع عليها.

sudan.title: مسيرات «الدعم السريع» تستهدف محطة كهرباء تندلتي وانقطاع التيار عن شمال كردفان - سودان تربيون
sudan.summary: استهدفت مسيرات قوات الدعم السريع محطة كهرباء تندلتي، مما أدى إلى انقطاع التيار الكهربائي عن مناطق واسعة في شمال كردفان. الحادثة تأتي في إطار تصاعد التوترات بين القوات المسلحة السودانية وقوات الدعم السريع، حيث تشهد البلاد صراعات مستمرة منذ فترة. وقد أثرت هذه الأحداث بشكل كبير على حياة المواطنين، حيث يعاني الكثيرون من انقطاع الكهرباء والمياه. السلطات المحلية تعمل على تقييم الأضرار واتخاذ الإجراءات اللازمة لاستعادة الخدمة.

sudan.title: سوق أميت تحت نيران المسيّرات: من يحمي المدنيين من امتداد الحرب السودانية؟ - سودانايل
sudan.summary: تتناول المقالة الوضع في سوق أميت، حيث تتعرض المنطقة لتهديدات متزايدة من المسيّرات في ظل تصاعد النزاع في السودان. تشير التقارير إلى أن المدنيين في المنطقة يعانون من مخاطر كبيرة نتيجة للاشتباكات المستمرة، مما يثير تساؤلات حول كيفية حماية هؤلاء المدنيين من تداعيات الحرب. تتناول المقالة أيضًا دور المجتمع الدولي والمحلي في تقديم الدعم والحماية للمدنيين، وتسلط الضوء على الحاجة الملحة لتوفير الأمن والاستقرار في المناطق المتأثرة بالنزاع. كما تناقش الأبعاد الإنسانية للأزمة وتأثيرها على حياة الناس في سوق أميت.

sudan.title: ماذا تريد الإمارات العربية المتحدة في السودان؟ - سودانايل
sudan.summary: تتناول المقالة دور الإمارات العربية المتحدة في السودان، حيث تسعى لتعزيز نفوذها في المنطقة من خلال استثمارات اقتصادية ودعم سياسي. تشير التقارير إلى أن الإمارات تهدف إلى تحقيق مصالح استراتيجية، تشمل تأمين موارد طبيعية وتعزيز الأمن الإقليمي. كما تبرز العلاقات بين الإمارات والسودان، والتي تشمل التعاون في مجالات مثل الزراعة والبنية التحتية. ومع ذلك، يواجه هذا التوجه تحديات، بما في ذلك الأوضاع السياسية المتقلبة في السودان والصراعات الداخلية. تسلط المقالة الضوء على كيفية تأثير هذه الديناميكيات على مستقبل العلاقات بين البلدين وأهداف الإمارات في تحقيق استقرار طويل الأمد في السودان.

ethiopia.title: PM Abiy Says Eritrean People Have Lost Former Assets Since Secession
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Says Eritrean People Have Lost Former Assets Since Secession - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Says Eritrean People Have Lost Former Assets Since Secession 20 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said Eritrean people have lost much of its industrial capacity and urban vitality since secession, urging good neighborliness and development cooperation as the path forward. During an interview with the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), the Prime Minister said Eritrean cities were once thriving economic centers when Eritrea was part of Ethiopia. However, these assets have significantly deteriorated since Eritrea's secession, with some cities losing much of their former urban character. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Recalling that Eritrea had more than 300 industries during that period, the Premier said the region had a substantial industrial base, contrasting its former economic strength with what he described as its present decline. Citing Asmara, PM Abiy said the capital had become smaller than many developing Ethiopian cities such as Arba Minch and Jigjiga. Speaking about the Red Sea port cities of Massawa and Assab, the Prime Minister said their economic activity had declined significantly, leaving their potential largely underutilized. "Massawa has been emptied, while Assab has been reduced to a ghost town," Prime Minister Abiy said. The Prime Minister attributed the situation to the Eritrean government's failure to prioritize development and institution-building, adding that its policies had instead drawn the country into serving the interests of forces opposed to Ethiopia. He said Eritreans, whom he described as industrious and welcoming, were now facing displacement and hardship, underscoring that external factors supporting confrontation would not resolve the country's underlying challenges. Such involvement, the Premier said, offers no lasting solution to Eritrea's problems, as those supporting confrontation are more likely to provide ammunition than contribute to addressing the country's difficulties. He stressed that friendship, good neighborliness and development cooperation remain the viable path forward, noting that decades of experience have demonstrated the limitations of alternative approaches. The Prime Minister warned that continued disregard for calls to pursue partnership and development, rather than allowing the region to become an arena for external rivalries, could have serious consequences. ethiopia.title: Eritrea's Migration Economy - Can the Nation Survive Without Forced Remittance?
ethiopia.content: Eritrea's Migration Economy - Can the Nation Survive Without Forced Remittance? - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Eritrea's Migration Economy - Can the Nation Survive Without Forced Remittance? 20 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) October 20, 2026 (ENA) Britain's October 2026 ultimatum to Eritrea exposed a long-standing contradiction at the heart of Isaias Afwerki's regime. The Asmara administration promotes self-reliance while rejecting fixed national budgets and external dependence. Yet, its system is sustained by the very forces it claims to transcend: indefinite national service drives emigration, while remittances from Eritreans abroad help finance the system that compels them to leave. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced that Eritrea faces a total visa ban for its nationals unless Asmara resumes cooperation on the return of failed asylum seekers and foreign national offenders. Preferential processing for officials has already been withdrawn, and diplomats have been placed under travel limits outside London. This announcement came at a moment when Eritreans formed the largest nationality among small-boat arrivals in the year to June 2026--roughly 5,875 recorded arrivals, or about 18 percent of the total--and ranked second in overall asylum claims, with initial grant rates near 83-84 percent. Although Eritrea dismissed the pressure as a "dismissible political gimmick," the sequence of events requires a closer examination of a political economy that has organized continuous emigration into a remittance resource. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn That political economy, controlled by Shabia under President Isaias Afwerki since independence, rests on three interlocking pillars: indefinite national service, party ownership of the command economy, and the systematic capture of external financial flows. While appearing distinct, these pillars function as a single mechanism that converts the population into both a captive labor force at home and a source of finance abroad. This framework structured itself around the continuous extraction of value from that emigration, yielding a sustained regime monopoly. Way back in 1997, Eritrea ratified a constitution that has remained unimplemented for nearly three decades. In 2001, independent media outlets were shut down after senior party figures called for democratic elections and constitutional enforcement. As a result, what was once framed as temporary wartime mobilization hardened into a permanent state architecture in which citizenship itself was redefined as an obligation rather than a right. Although national service was formally limited to 18 months under Proclamation 82/1995, it has operated without an end date since the 1998-2000 border war. Secondary school students complete their final year at the Sawa military training center before being assigned to military or civilian roles that can last for decades, earning a meager stipend of 450 to 500 Nakfa a month--roughly 30 USD. Conditions like these are what the UN Commission of Inquiry characterized as "slavery-like," linking them to arbitrary detention and the collective punishment of families. Such practices drive continuous emigration, where the outflow is not a policy failure but rather a deliberate revenue stream. While resident population estimates hover around 3.6 million, diaspora figures range from roughly 600,000 to 900,000 registered migrants and refugees, with up to one-third of the Eritrean-born population living outside the country. According to UNHCR data for the end of 2025, there were roughly 555,000 refugees plus more than 118,000 asylum seekers--totaling approximately 670,000-679,000 people of concern--with new asylum applications in 2025 alone exceeding 53,000. Although the formal economy remains dominated by Shabia-linked enterprises and the state, private-sector activity outside small family trade is constrained by currency controls, licensing restrictions, and the national-service labor regime. The decisive resource is human capital exported and then taxed; most household survival depends on external transfers estimated at 200 to 300 million USD annually--equivalent to roughly 30 percent of Eritrea's GDP. These flows keep households solvent in an environment of limited domestic opportunity, while a parallel 2 percent diaspora tax is levied on Eritreans abroad and collected through embassies and informal networks. Economic ownership is concentrated in party-controlled structures: the Hidri Trust functions as the central holding vehicle for Shabia's commercial interests, the Red Sea Trading Corporation holds an effective monopoly on significant imports and serves as a primary channel for foreign exchange, construction firms such as Segen and Bidho execute major works frequently using national-service labor, and Himbol Financial Services manages remittances and related transactions. State banks exist, yet the party retains parallel financial channels outside conventional budgetary oversight, amidst no comprehensive national budget having been published since independence. This dual extraction reduces the need for productive employment creation and creates a closed loop in which indefinite national service and political controls generate flight, which in turn generates remittances and state revenue. When compared to the official doctrine of self-reliance that Eritrea follows--which rejects aid dependency while treating citizens as both free labor and external financiers--isolation from conventional multilateral finance is justified, while political pluralism is framed as a threat to national unity and sovereignty. This produces a distinctive equilibrium in which political power is monopolized, and the regime's authority on budgets and the precise size of party holdings stay outside public scrutiny. Eritrea's migration economy is therefore not an unintended by-product of isolation, but the operating logic of a political order that converts its people into the principal resource keeping the regime intact. The Eritrean government, led by President Isaias Afwerki, promotes self-reliance while simultaneously depending on financial flows from citizens abroad, which are crucial for the regime's survival. A recent ultimatum from the UK threatens visa bans unless Eritrea cooperates on returning failed asylum seekers, highlighting the contradiction in its policies. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Signs Second-Phase LNG Development Deal for Ogaden Gas Field
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Signs Second-Phase LNG Development Deal for Ogaden Gas Field - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Signs Second-Phase LNG Development Deal for Ogaden Gas Field 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Chinese companies GCL Group and Jurong Group have signed an agreement to develop the second phase of a liquefied natural gas (LNG) project at Ethiopia's Calub gas field in the Somali Region, as the government seeks to expand commercial use of the country's natural gas reserves. The agreement, signed on 16 October at the Ministry of Mines in Addis Abeba in the presence of Mines Minister Alemtsehay Paulos, covers engineering, construction and natural gas liquefaction and processing services. It follows a strategic cooperation framework signed by the two companies in May 2026 and the commissioning of the project's first phase in October 2025. According to Seetao, the first phase consists of a modular LNG facility designed to process 200,000 cubic metres of natural gas daily, producing approximately 50,000 metric tonnes of LNG annually, primarily for domestic industrial consumers. The second phase is intended to increase production and serve international markets, although the companies have not disclosed the contract value, additional processing capacity or completion timeline. The agreement comes amid renewed efforts to commercialise the Ogaden Basin's gas resources after years of delays. In March 2026, GCL and Dangote Group signed a reported $4.2 billion , 25-year gas supply agreement for a urea fertiliser complex in Gode, with plans to transport gas from Calub through a pipeline of approximately 108-110 kilometres. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Poly-GCL, associated with GCL's wider corporate group, has operated in the basin since 2013 under production-sharing agreements covering the Calub and Hilala fields. Ethiopia's government terminated the company's contracts in September 2022 following disputes over capital registration, outstanding fees and delays in development, before reversing the decision in June 2024. In August 2022, Ethiopia received its first gas reserves certificate, confirming an estimated seven trillion cubic feet of natural gas in the Ogaden Basin, according to a study by Netherland, Sewell & Associates. Despite the renewed investment push, export arrangements for the LNG project remain unclear. Ethiopia is landlocked, and earlier proposals to transport gas to Djibouti for export have not resulted in a publicly confirmed export route for the second phase. The agreement's financing, delivery schedule and intended international buyers have also not been announced. Read the original article on Addis Standard . ethiopia.title: PM Abiy Warns Eritrea of 'Extremely Severe' Consequences If It Rejects Ethiopia's Peace Call Amid Rising Tensions
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Warns Eritrea of 'Extremely Severe' Consequences If It Rejects Ethiopia's Peace Call Amid Rising Tensions - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Warns Eritrea of 'Extremely Severe' Consequences If It Rejects Ethiopia's Peace Call Amid Rising Tensions 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has warned Eritrea of "extremely severe" consequences if its government continues to reject Ethiopia's calls for peace and regional cooperation, accusing Asmara of aligning itself with forces seeking to destabilize Ethiopia. He also called on Tigrayan youth to abandon armed struggle, accusing Tigrayan People's Liberation Front (TPLF) leaders of prolonging conflict at the expense of the region's population. In a Tigrigna-language interview with the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), Abiy said Eritrea should pursue economic development and cooperation with Ethiopia rather than serve as a haven for forces hostile to the country. "Rather than becoming a development partner, choosing to be a haven for enemies is not beneficial; ignoring our call for peace, however, will carry extremely severe consequences," he said. Abiy criticized Eritrea's economic conditions, contrasting the country's present state with its industrial and commercial activity before independence. He claimed that Asmara had diminished in stature, Massawa remained in ruins, and Assab had become a wasteland, arguing that Eritrea's population had lost much of what it gained after independence. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines He accused Eritrea's ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), which he referred to as Shaebia, of prioritizing regional destabilization over domestic development. He maintained that Ethiopia remained committed to peace and joint development but warned that continued rejection of its appeals would have serious consequences. The remarks come amid heightened tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, alongside renewed fighting and political uncertainty in northern Ethiopia. Relations between the two countries have deteriorated amid disagreements over regional security and Ethiopia's pursuit of access to the Red Sea. Addressing the situation in Tigray, Abiy said the federal government would support the region's reconstruction, lasting peace, and economic recovery. He urged residents to protect their institutions and work with federal and regional security structures until an elected administration is established through a free and democratic vote. He called on Tigrayan youth involved in armed movements to lay down their weapons and enter the disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration (DDR) process. He also urged military and political leaders to surrender peacefully, saying, "Enough is enough; peace is better." Abiy accused TPLF leaders of sending young people to fight while their families live abroad or in Addis Abeba and they accumulate wealth. He contrasted their circumstances with those of young Tigrayans who, he said, have suffered death, physical disabilities, and psychological trauma from successive rounds of fighting. The message to young people is clear: you too can help build Kenya," he added. Abiy's remarks placed young people at the center of Kenya's development agenda, at a time when employment creation, enterprise growth and access to economic opportunities remain important policy priorities. Kenya's youth population presents both an opportunity for economic expansion and a challenge for policymakers, particularly as young people seek formal employment, financing for businesses and pathways into productive sectors of the economy. The Ethiopian leader said building successful nations required patience and investment in institutions capable of serving citizens, while giving young people the support needed to shape their futures. His remarks underscored the role of education, public service, entrepreneurship and creative industries in national development, broadening the definition of heroism beyond those recognized for political and historical contributions. ethiopia.title: Somalia's Aid Paradox - Saving Lives, Sustaining Dependency
ethiopia.content: Somalia's Aid Paradox - Saving Lives, Sustaining Dependency - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Somalia's Aid Paradox - Saving Lives, Sustaining Dependency 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — For more than three decades, international aid has been an indispensable lifeline for Somalia. It has helped prevent humanitarian collapse, funded essential health and education services, and sustained civil-society organizations through cycles of conflict, drought, and displacement. Those contributions are real and should never be minimized. Yet prolonged reliance on external assistance raises a challenging political-economy question: can a humanitarian and development apparatus designed for immediate rescue inadvertently entrench the political arrangements and structural fragilities that perpetuate dependency? This is not an argument that external assistance has failed uniformly, that donors harbor designs to sustain instability, or that Somali institutions are passive actors. Nor does it suggest that all aid is diverted or that humanitarian organizations ignore accountability. Such sweeping claims would exceed the available evidence. The more useful inquiry concerns incentives: who sets funding priorities, who controls resources and acquires lasting capacity, who benefits commercially and politically, how much say citizens have over resources meant for them, and what happens when funding priorities change faster than public institutions can adapt. These questions are now time-sensitive because international funding is shrinking while domestic needs remain acute. The International Monetary Fund's 2025 review of Somalia estimated, from available donor information, that foreign aid may have amounted to roughly 20-30% of GDP over the preceding decade. It cautioned that comprehensive official records of total aid flows were unavailable and that most assistance was delivered outside the government budget. It also modeled possible 2025 reductions of $400-600 million, about 3-4.6% of GDP. Those were scenarios based on anticipated cuts and disbursement delays, not a measurement of every dollar ultimately lost. The World Bank's Toward Building Somalia's Social Contract adds the fiscal picture. For 2022, the federal government collected about $262 million in domestic revenue, 2.2% of GDP, while external grants financed 62% of federal spending, and 82% of official development assistance was off-budget. These are 2022 figures, not a description of Somalia's fiscal position today, but they show how thin the domestic revenue base was relative to public responsibilities. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The Overseas Development Institute's April 2026 study, Somali Systems: From Aid-Centred to State-Led Crisis Response , brings the concern into current policy. The authors of the study, Surer Mohamed and Dustin Barter, argue that the outsized role of aid and the incentives around its delivery can impede a move to state-led crisis response. They acknowledge the risks of weak transparency, accountability, and inclusion in state-led arrangements but conclude that keeping the aid-centred status quo carries greater long-term risk. As Somalia confronts shrinking funding alongside acute need, dissecting the anatomy of its aid economy is no longer only an academic exercise; it is a practical policy priority. The question is not aid versus no aid. It is whether assistance can save lives today while building the accountable institutions, domestic revenue, and public capabilities that make tomorrow's recovery less dependent on external decisions. Anatomy of aid economy Foreign assistance is rarely neutral. It is a system of decisions about authority, policy direction, and resource distribution. When external actors set funding priorities, approve project designs and manage disbursement channels, they exercise considerable influence over domestic public administration. That influence is not automatically improper. Donors answer to taxpayers and legislatures, international organizations must meet fiduciary and safeguarding standards, and humanitarian agencies need flexibility to reach people in territories where state authority is limited. Aid should not be judged solely by what it delivers today, but by the institutions and capabilities it leaves behind." In Somalia, however, the cumulative result is a crowded institutional landscape of fragmented project delivery. A donor may channel funds through an international agency, which contracts a national NGO, which then negotiates local access through customary or community intermediaries. Meanwhile, the line ministry retains only partial visibility into actual expenditure, geographic coverage, or long-term operating costs. Each link in the chain can fulfill its contractual obligations while the system as a whole remains difficult for citizens to understand or hold to account. Across health, education, water, nutrition, livelihoods, and local governance, three recurring features characterize the aid economy. The first is fragmented standards, wherein parallel project frameworks operate on different procurement rules, reporting formats, and salary scales, and because staff are trained for a project but are rarely absorbed into a lasting institutional structure, administrative capacity does not accumulate where it is most needed. The second is data isolation, where monitoring information is often routed into donor reports rather than integrated into national information systems, preventing governments from easily planning, coordinating, or evaluating. The third is vulnerable continuity, which means that services expand while a grant is active and become fragile when it closes, leaving ministries with commitments they did not choose and cannot finance. This pattern is consistent with the wider scholarship. Ken Menkhaus's work on aid and institution-building highlights the difficulty of building durable institutions through fragmented, project-based interventions, while Tobias Hagmann's Stabilization, Extraversion and Political Settlements in Somalia examines how external intervention interacts with domestic political authority. Aid also operates inside a delicate political settlement that involves the federal government, federal member states, local administrations, customary authorities, clan networks, and commercial interests. Money entering that environment interacts with existing power relationships. Its effects depend not only on the objectives written in project documents but also on who controls access, receives contracts, influences beneficiary selection, gains employment, and acquires political visibility. Aid should therefore be judged by two separate questions. First, what goods, services, and humanitarian outcomes does it deliver? Second, what political, commercial, and institutional relationships does the way it is delivered create or reinforce? A program can meet its targets and still leave little institutional legacy. An emergency response can rightly put speed above institution-building. The task is to distinguish legitimate emergency arrangements from avoidable, permanent dependency. The Bypassing Dilemma: State-building without the state Donors face a recurring choice: channel funds through public institutions burdened by capacity gaps and security risks, or deliver through international agencies with insulated risk-management systems. In acute crises, bypassing the state is often defensible. Public money should not be exposed to unacceptable risk merely to demonstrate national ownership, and life-saving relief cannot always wait for better audit or procurement systems. The damage arises when a temporary workaround hardens into permanent architecture. Repeated bypassing deprives ministries of the experience they need in procurement, program management, monitoring, and service delivery. They lack reliable expenditure data, struggle to coordinate interventions funded elsewhere, and cannot estimate the recurrent costs that follow a project's end. A self-reinforcing cycle results in three main stages. The first stage is perceived weakness, where limited administrative reach encourages donors to bypass state mechanisms. The second stage is deprived experience, in which bypassing denies ministries the opportunities to manage resources and deliver services. The third stage is perpetual fragility, where this persistent weakness is subsequently cited to justify continued circumvention. Breaking the cycle requires reciprocal commitments. Somali institutions must demonstrate fiscal integrity, keep reliable financial records, enforce procurement standards, and accept independent oversight; where they do not, external caution is legitimate. International partners, for their part, cannot expect national institutions to mature while indefinitely reserving the most consequential management functions for themselves. They should build capacity and expenditure transparency into off-budget programs from the start. The World Bank's Somalia Financial Governance Report 2025 , disclosed on 30 September 2026, examines revenue administration, public procurement, financial-sector oversight, petroleum governance, and emerging fiscal pressures, including security-sector costs. These are precisely the functions that determine whether Somalia can responsibly manage more of its own public resources over time. The strategic question is not whether all assistance should flow through government tomorrow. It is whether each off-budget program has a clear justification, a defined link to national priorities, adequate expenditure visibility, and a realistic plan to strengthen Somali capacity where appropriate. A health donor, for instance, could disclose implementing institutions, districts covered, spending categories, duration, and expected recurrent costs, while the ministry helps set service standards and reviews performance even if the donor retains financial control. A civil-service reform program should be judged not by workshops delivered but by whether recruitment becomes more competitive, payroll and personnel records improve, and essential functions continue after the project closes. Ownership vs Control: Moving beyond declarations International frameworks routinely champion national ownership; Somalia's New Deal Compact was one expression of that ambition. Yet the term can mean very different things: a government endorsing a strategy, ministries joining program design, Somali institutions controlling expenditure, or citizens and legislators shaping and scrutinizing priorities. These are not equivalent, and the first is far easier to achieve than the last. A government can endorse a national development plan while lacking influence over the resources needed to implement it. A ministry can attend coordination meetings without controlling a single funding decision. A national strategy can become the reference document for dozens of projects while nobody holds reliable information on their combined spending or future operating costs. Ownership then remains a political declaration rather than an operational capability. The gap widens when donors operate across different geographic zones, apply separate funding cycles and reporting rules, and work around federal ministries. Each project may be individually defensible, yet the collective pattern is uneven: one district receives overlapping interventions while another is underserved, and a ministry with a national mandate lacks the staff to coordinate externally financed work. Federalism adds a further layer, because member states may receive assistance through several international channels, complicating coordination between national and subnational levels. None of this requires bad faith. Organizations rationally pursue their own mandates, yet the combined outcome is less effective than a coordinated one. A more substantive definition of ownership is needed, anchored in demonstrable influence over planning, transparent expenditure tracking, and public accountability. At the same time, ownership cannot be a euphemism for unaccountable political control over donor resources. A credible national system requires transparent procurement, legislative scrutiny, independent oversight, and genuine avenues for citizens to participate and to challenge decisions. The aim is not to swap donor control for unaccountable domestic control but to allocate responsibilities clearly and hold both domestic and international actors to their commitments. Fiscal Foundations: Reconnecting revenue to social contract Taxation is more than a way of raising money; it is part of the fiscal cement that binds citizens to the state. Taxpayers have a stronger claim to explanations about spending and service quality, and governments that depend on domestic revenue have stronger reasons to engage constructively with taxpayers and the businesses that sustain the economy. Taxation does not automatically produce democracy, and domestic revenue can itself be captured by political or commercial interests. Even so, the link between revenue and accountability matters for Somalia's state-building debate. The question is not aid versus no aid, but whether assistance can save lives today while building institutions that make tomorrow's recovery less dependent on external decisions." The 2022 World Bank figures cited above illustrate the historical imbalance: federal domestic revenue of about 2.2% of GDP, combined federal and member-state revenue of about 3.6%, and external grants financing 62% of federal expenditure. When public services are financed by actors who are not answerable to domestic political processes, the feedback loop between taxation, representation, and accountability remains underdeveloped. Citizens may not know which institution is responsible for a service, and government may be blamed for failures it has no means to prevent. The problem is not simply that Somalia collects too little tax. It is whether the collection is equitable, predictable, transparent, and tied to visible improvements in services. Where households and businesses face multiple charges, informal payments, or unpredictable levies while public services remain weak, taxation deepens distrust rather than building the social contract. Somalia, therefore, needs a dual reform: expanding lawful domestic revenue while making its use more transparent and responsive to public needs. Somaliland offers a useful but qualified comparison. In Taxation, Political Accountability and Foreign Aid: Lessons from Somaliland , Nicholas Eubank argued that Somaliland's limited access to foreign assistance increased the importance of local tax revenue and gave actors outside government leverage to demand more inclusive and accountable institutions. Sarah Phillips's When Less Was More likewise stresses the role of local ownership in the formative settlement, while noting the exclusionary limits of elite bargaining. Later scholarship, such as Somaliland's Authoritarian Turn , documents the risks of oligarchic influence and concentrated economic power. The lesson is not that less aid automatically produces better governance. Somaliland's path reflected a distinctive history of conflict, customary negotiation, and local institution-building, and limited aid was one factor among several. A sudden reduction in Somalia could devastate essential services without producing more representative institutions. The comparison is best treated as a hypothesis about revenue bargaining, namely that stronger domestic mobilization, combined with transparent spending and meaningful participation, can create a more durable basis for accountability. Managing Vulnerability: Gatekeeping, diversion risks Humanitarian operations function in environments where access often depends on negotiation with regional authorities, landowners, customary leaders, and commercial intermediaries. These relationships can be vital for safe passage, staff protection, and community acceptance, and local knowledge is often indispensable. But they also create risks of exclusion, manipulation, and diversion. The question is how systems of access and influence affect who actually receives what has been allocated. The independent Inter-Agency Humanitarian Evaluation of the Response to the Humanitarian Crisis in Somalia , published in 2025 (see also the UNFPA overview ), assessed the collective famine-prevention response of 2021-2024. It found that the scaled-up response played a critical role in preventing famine and saving lives. It also identified weaknesses in accountability, inclusion, coordination, and the management of diversion risk, noting that the rapid expansion of assistance in 2022 initially gave insufficient attention to the growing risk of diversion. Later reforms improved cooperation and transparency but took longer than envisaged. The evaluation further noted that the full 2023 post-distribution diversion investigation remained confidential, with access limited to selected stakeholders. Confidentiality can be justified to protect investigations, personal safety, or due process, but it is a transparency issue worth recognizing. These findings must be read carefully, as they show that diversion risks were serious enough to warrant investigation and system-wide reform, but they do not show that every program was compromised or that diversion occurred at the same scale everywhere. Three structural vulnerabilities stand out. The first is initial blind spots, where rapid scale-ups during acute crises can underestimate and under-manage escalating diversion risk. The second is registration challenges, in which digital beneficiary registries can improve auditing and prevent duplication, but if selection itself reflects unequal access to local power, technology can make an exclusionary allocation more efficient because better data cannot show whether the criteria are fair. The third is oversight gaps, meaning that third-party monitoring must go beyond confirming that goods reached a location and should instead verify that recipients received their full entitlements, that no unauthorized deductions occurred, that people were not excluded because of identity or status, and that complaints can be made safely. The World Food Programme's 2024 targeting pilots in Baidoa and Dolow, discussed in a December 2025 ODI report , explored ways to improve targeting and protect the integrity of unconditional cash and voucher assistance. Their lesson is that integrity depends on attention to power, not merely on better forms, software, and audit procedures. Commercial rents, political competition A large injection of foreign aid also creates demand for logistics, transport, security, construction, communications, consultancy, and financial services. These markets create jobs and stimulate local economic activity. They can also concentrate benefits among narrow networks with privileged access to information and decision-makers. Somalia's wider political economy sharpens the point. Movement corridors, ports, checkpoints, and aid procurement can generate substantial income entangled with political and security arrangements. PeaceRep's September 2026 analysis, "A Decade on, Somalia's Federal Pact Benefits Elites and Al-Shabaab ," draws on several hundred interviews across Somalia and the diaspora. It identifies two connected themes: control of movement through checkpoints and control, mismanagement, or manipulation of international aid. Its authors argue that political elites and business allies can profit from aid-related rents and economic chokepoints. These are the researchers' interpretations of their evidence, not proof that every official, business, or aid organization is implicated. Further material is available on PeaceRep's Somalia page . However, this prolonged dependency raises concerns about whether such aid inadvertently reinforces political fragility and hinders the development of local institutions. The International Monetary Fund has highlighted that foreign aid constituted 20-30% of Somalia's GDP in recent years, with a significant portion delivered off-budget, complicating accountability and governance. As international funding declines, the challenge is to balance immediate humanitarian needs with the necessity of building sustainable local capacities. Studies suggest that while bypassing state mechanisms may be necessary in crises, it can lead to a cycle of dependency and institutional weakness. To break this cycle, both Somali institutions and international donors must commit to enhancing fiscal integrity and transparency, ensuring that aid not only addresses immediate needs but also fosters long-term resilience and governance.

ethiopia.title: From Military Victory to Political Settlement - Why Ethiopia's Real Test Lies Beyond Controlling Mekelle
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: From Military Victory to Political Settlement - Why Ethiopia's Real Test Lies Beyond Controlling Mekelle - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: From Military Victory to Political Settlement - Why Ethiopia's Real Test Lies Beyond Controlling Mekelle 19 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Mekelle, the capital of Tigray Regional State, has now changed hands three times in six years. Federal forces took the city in November 2020, within a month of the last war beginning; Tigrayan forces retook it in June 2021 . On 3 October 2026, federal troops and the allied Tigray Peace Force entered it again , after the TPLF announced that it had withdrawn and that its regional administration would "temporarily move out" of the capital. The mood in parts of Addis Abeba is triumphant. It should be sober. This round began on 23 September, when Tigrayan forces launched an offensive into Afar and Amhara . The momentum soon reversed; government-aligned forces have since also entered Adigrat , near the Eritrean border, and Axum . On 11 October, according to local media, Getachew Reda, now the prime minister's adviser on East African affairs, declared the war over and said Tigray would be run by a federal command post for six months before elections. The TPLF leadership, now in the northern countryside, has announced a shift to "mobile warfare." Taking a city is a military event. Settling the question that produced the war is sociological: who belongs to the political community, on what terms, and who has the authority to decide. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines My argument is this. The war is rooted in an unresolved bargain at home; the regional realignment that now sets rival Gulf- and Egypt-led alignments against each other across the Horn raises its stakes and supplies its patrons. Ethiopia is stronger in external terms than at any point since 2018, yet thinner in the social foundations of authority: the willing consent of its own regions. Whether Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed emerges as the Horn's pivotal statesman or as the manager of a permanent counterinsurgency depends on what Addis Abeba does with Mekelle, not on the fact of having taken it. Tigray's unfinished peace, Ethiopia's unsettled state The federal government's case deserves to be stated at full strength, because much of it is sound. The Pretoria Agreement of 2022 required the disarmament of Tigrayan forces, and disputes over disarmament and the TPLF's legal status were never resolved . In 2025 a TPLF faction forced Getachew Reda out of the interim administration ; in May 2026 the party reinstated the pre-war regional council, which elected Debretsion Gebremichael as president , outside the framework Pretoria had set. By mid-year, Tigray's authorities were declaring that the agreement "has collapsed," and on 23 September, it was Tigrayan forces that went on the offensive. No sovereign state tolerates a second army answering to a rival government. That case is strong, but it is not the whole account. A detailed Al Jazeera reconstruction found that while the TPLF retained an organizational and security role the agreement was meant to diminish , the federal government also failed to deliver important parts of the settlement. The June national elections were not held in Tigray at all . Meanwhile, Tigrayans lived what a contributor in these pages called peace on paper and suffering in practice . By May, Addis Standard was reporting allegations of forced conscription across Tigray , with opposition parties such as Salsay Weyane Tigray demanding an end to what Tigrayans call gifa. Prolonged deprivation converts political grievance into everyday humiliation, the raw material of mobilization. Tigrayan dissent also shows that Tigray is not a single political subject. Any settlement that treats the TPLF as the sole voice of Tigray, or all Tigrayans as the TPLF, will misread the society it seeks to pacify. Taking a city is a military event. Settling the question that produced the war is sociological." By September, Ethiopia contained two authorities claiming to govern the same territory, each with its own army. Charles Tilly called this condition multiple sovereignty and treated it as the defining feature of a revolutionary situation. The war is therefore less about resources or ideology than about statehood: whether Ethiopia's federation is a union of self-governing nations that may bargain with the center by force or a sovereign state that monopolizes legitimate coercion and negotiates only through its institutions. Alliance of the aggrieved Days before the offensive, seven armed movements, including the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Oromo Liberation Army, announced an alliance pledging to work toward the fall of Abiy's government and its replacement by a charter-based transitional administration. Fano fought alongside federal forces against the TPLF in 2020-2022 , and Amhara and Tigrayan nationalists still claim the same land in Western Tigray. Sociologically, this is a negative coalition, bound by a shared adversary rather than a shared vision. Such coalitions are strong at the moment of mobilization and brittle at the moment of distribution, because what each member ultimately wants is indivisible: Welkait cannot belong to both Amhara and Tigray. The fissures also run through, not merely between, these constituencies. The Tigray Peace Force, a Tigrayan militia aligned with Addis Abeba , helped take Alamata and entered Mekelle beside federal troops, and Getachew Reda, once the TPLF's most visible spokesman, returned to the city as the face of federal authority. The war over Tigray is also, increasingly, a war within it. Yet a fractious coalition is not an impotent one. Fano holds towns in southern Wollo and northern Shewa , and the TPLF left Mekelle without a street battle, preserving its fighters, much as it withdrew to the highlands in 2020 before returning in 2021. Analysts at the Critical Threats Project judge the movement weaker than in the last war , citing thinner popular support and Ethiopia's improved drones. They may be right. But insurgencies need not win battles; they need only outlast a state's patience. After Mekelle: Control without consent The capture of Mekelle by federal forces has not ended multiple sovereignty; it has changed its form. Two governments in one region have become a government in the towns and an insurgency in the hills. The question now is whether the authority that holds Mekelle can become one Tigrayans obey without being compelled. The first days show how steep that climb will be. Federal forces did not inherit a city ready to be governed. Residents described a security vacuum and looting of government offices , and the UN reported that warehouses run by a UN agency and aid organizations had been looted . The fighting has been costly: hospital sources told the BBC that at least 52 civilians were killed in three days around Alamata , and a humanitarian source estimated at least 150,000 displaced in Afar . All this falls on a region already in drought, where, according to the regional disaster agency, 3.9 million people, more than half the population, needed emergency food assistance . An administration that arrives by arms will be judged by bread, and it will be judged quickly. A command post followed by elections has a logic, but it is an instrument of what sociologist Michael Mann called despotic power , the capacity to act without negotiating with society. Despotic power can take a city; only infrastructural power, the routine capacity to deliver law and services with local cooperation, can hold it. The Tigray Peace Force gives the federal presence a Tigrayan face, but it also risks turning a federal-regional war into an intra-Tigrayan one, in which those who fought beside Addis Abeba are seen by their neighbors as agents of conquest. Success over the next six months will be measured not in towns held but in whether cash, fuel, and food move; whether the displaced of Western Tigray can go home; and whether Tigrayans who belong to neither the TPLF nor the Tigray Peace Force can organize, compete, and win. Mandate and monopoly The Prosperity Party comfortably won June's elections , taking 438 of the 486 seats for which results were declared . The vote supplied a procedural mandate. It could not, by itself, supply what Max Weber treated as the substance of legitimacy: a belief among the governed that authority is rightful. Elections were not held in Tigray, Fano has held swathes of the Amhara countryside since 2023 , and the OLA has fought in Oromia since 2018. Before the vote, an Addis Standard op-ed described the ruling party's method as procedural authoritarianism , power exercised through rather than against formal institutions. Where institutions cannot carry competition, it migrates to arms. The National Dialogue Commission might have been a bridge, yet even its Tigray agenda-gathering forum had to be moved to Addis Abeba . Battlefield success can deepen state authority; Tilly's observation that war made the state is not wrong. But in Ethiopia, war has unmade regimes as often as it has made them; the Derg fell to a coalition of regional fronts. The temptation after Mekelle will be to treat armed opponents purely as criminals rather than as expressions of unresolved political questions. A Tigray election held under a command post, without credible guarantees for the TPLF's rivals or a path back for its rank and file, would reproduce the June pattern at regional scale: a mandate without consent. Abiy's two ledgers The external ledger is strong. In June, the IMF reported improving output, exports, reserves, and revenue, alongside declining inflation , as it reached agreement on the fifth review of Ethiopia's program. By external measures, Abiy is stronger than at any point in his tenure. The domestic ledger is harder. The coalition now arrayed against him includes his two most important wartime partners of 2020: Fano and Eritrea. Supporters of the government will say each broke away over its own ambitions: Fano over the reorganization of regional special forces , Asmara over a Pretoria process to which it was not a party . Critics see a pattern in which alliances rest on personal bargains rather than institutions and dissolve once those bargains are spent. Either way, Ethiopia's wartime friendships have proved less durable than its enmities. The 2019 Nobel laureate, honored for making peace with Eritrea, now accuses Asmara of sending troops into Tigray. In a February letter to Addis Standard, former foreign minister Gedu Andargachew said that Eritrean and Ethiopian forces operated "as a single force" until the Pretoria ceasefire , an account that contradicts the prime minister's own. An unreckoned war tends to seed the next one. If military advantage is now followed by political inclusion, Abiy will emerge as the Horn's indispensable statesman. If it is followed by reprisal and exclusion, he risks winning a war and losing the peace for a second time. Access to the sea and the logic of encirclement No issue has shaped the regional reading of this war more than Abiy's quest for the sea. He has called the loss of Assab a historical mistake whose reversal is "a matter of time," while insisting that Ethiopia has no intention to invade Eritrea . The war has turned that ambition into a concrete vulnerability. Fighting in Afar threatened the routes from Djibouti through which most Ethiopian imports, including fuel, pass . A state of Ethiopia's size that depends on a single corridor through a contested borderland is not simply a trading nation with a logistics problem; it is a sovereignty with a hostage. Since Mekelle fell, the Eritrean dimension has moved from allegation towards confrontation. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of a territorial incursion and demanded the withdrawal of its troops and told the UN Security Council that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 kilometers into Tigray . Asmara denies any incursion and has asked the Council to intervene , calling Ethiopia's conduct a pretext to seize Assab. The scale of any Eritrean deployment has not been independently established. But on 5 October, in his re-inauguration address, Abiy reiterated that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea . Maritime access, national security, and the war have fused into one question. Addis Abeba's practical response has been quieter than its rhetoric and probably wiser. On 24 September, Abiy stood beside Djibouti's President Ismail Omar Guelleh to announce a $660 million refined-fuel pipeline from Damerjog to Dewele . The pipeline makes a neighbor a stakeholder in Ethiopia's security rather than an object of its ambition. This magazine warned in 2024 that a country ravaged by internal crises can neither shape nor safeguard its national interest . The most serious threat to Ethiopia's maritime lifeline in 2026 has come not from foreign navies but from fighting in Afar, Amhara, and Tigray. Sea access is a legitimate national aspiration, but its first line of defense runs through domestic peace. Two blocs, both fluid Those coastal anxieties have found patrons. The Institute for Economics and Peace describes an emerging UAE-Israel-Ethiopia axis set against a Saudi-Egypt-Türkiye reaction . In July, Saudi Arabia launched a 14-nation Red Sea maritime coalition that included Egypt, Türkiye, Sudan, Djibouti, and Somalia, but not the UAE. On 4 October, the day after Mekelle fell, the leaders of Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia, and Sudan converged at El Alamein; their declaration did not name Ethiopia but asserted that Red Sea governance belongs to littoral states and restated Egypt's demands on the dam . Sudan is where the blocs collide. Sudan's army-aligned government has alleged that drone attacks on its territory originated from Ethiopia , which Addis Abeba rejects as baseless , and a Reuters investigation reported that Ethiopia was hosting an RSF training camp . Ethiopia's army chief, in turn, accuses foreign powers of "pushing, supporting, and supplying" the new alliance , naming Eritrea, Sudan, and Egypt, all of which deny it. On 1 October, Ethiopia closed its embassy in Eritrea and expelled Eritrean diplomats ; Asmara severed relations . Whatever the truth of each allegation, proxy war is a currency that circulates in both directions. Ethiopia has won wars before. What it has rarely done is win the peace that follows." The Nile runs through the same ledger. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam was inaugurated in September 2025 , and in February Cairo denied a report that it had offered to help Ethiopia secure Red Sea access in exchange for flexibility on the dam. The two dossiers have become one bargaining space. No battle changes hydrology; what war changes is the cost of Egyptian pressure. If Ethiopia emerges cohesive, pressure exerted through its internal fault lines loses value. If the war drags on, Cairo gains leverage without firing a shot. These alignments are not alliances. Somalia joined the El Alamein summit yet kept cooperating with Addis Abeba, and its president met Abiy as recently as 28 September . Ethiopia's BRICS membership, shared with Egypt and the UAE , is insurance, not protection. Washington, which let its Eritrea sanctions lapse, citing US interests in the Red Sea while also imposing visa restrictions on "hardline members" of the TPLF , offers neutrality, not guarantees. Neither camp can impose an order on the Horn. The decisive variable is Ethiopia's internal cohesion: a united Ethiopia is a regional pole; a divided one is a regional battlefield. The first is coerced consolidation, and it is now the government's declared path: a command post, a coalition fragmenting along its fault lines, and separate settlements with its members. It can succeed only if it brings a credible process on the disputed territories, reconstruction, an election open to Tigrayans of every persuasion, and a national dialogue that includes those who fought. That requires a political generosity the government has not yet demonstrated. The second is protracted insurgency. The TPLF has given up the towns, not the war. Its leaders have promised further operations from the northern highlands, the terrain from which it returned in 2021. A mobile campaign alongside Fano and the OLA would mean a war of attrition that drains the economy and invites proxy intervention. The third is regionalization, and it is no longer hypothetical: severed diplomatic relations, rival letters to the Security Council, and reported Eritrean deployments on Ethiopian soil, layered onto Sudan's war. The EU has urged both governments to de-escalate , and the International Crisis Group has called for former AU envoy Olusegun Obasanjo to be brought back into mediation and for Saudi Arabia and the UAE to coordinate to keep a Red Sea front from opening. The fourth is a positive-sum Ethiopia. It reaches the sea not by redrawing borders but by rewriting interests: a guaranteed port and corridor arrangement in which Eritrea keeps sovereignty, Ethiopia holds equity and access, and neighbors share in its markets. The dam generated 52 percent of Ethiopia's electricity-export revenue in 2025/26 , according to the state utility; the planned Bishoftu airport is billed as Africa's largest ; and a population of some 135 million could make Ethiopia the Horn's energy, logistics, and manufacturing center. The current confrontation makes this harder, not impossible, provided Addis Abeba trades the language of restitution for that of interdependence. Without peace, a young population becomes a recruiting pool rather than a dividend. The darker variant of success is a garrison state with a port: a coastline without peace, power without legitimacy. Decisive Victory: Political, not military The strongest possibility is a civic turn. Both camps in this war are multi-ethnic coalitions, each discovering that no ethnic project can secure itself alone. Sea-access nationalism already addresses citizens as Ethiopians rather than as members of ethnic nations, but it cannot substitute for a negotiated federal bargain. Exhaustion, a generation born after 1991 and integrating national markets, could yield a different consensus: citizenship as the basis of political claims, cultural rights protected, Article 39 reinterpreted by agreement, electoral rules rewarding cross-regional parties, and disputed territories under shared administration. Imposed from above, civic nationalism becomes assimilation; it must be chosen, in Renan's phrase, as a daily plebiscite. The balance of power in the Horn will not finally be decided at Assab, at the dam, or in Mekelle. It will be decided by whether the Ethiopian state can turn the loyalty of its citizens from a battlefield into a resource. This is the paradox of Ethiopian power: the more Ethiopia acts as a regional power, the more its internal fault lines become assets for its rivals. Abiy has shown he can survive, outmaneuver, and project; the question is whether he can include. Ethiopia has won wars before. What it has rarely done is win the peace that follows. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's recent military control of Mekelle, the capital of Tigray, marks a significant shift in the ongoing conflict, which has seen the city change hands multiple times since 2020. Federal forces, alongside the Tigray Peace Force, re-entered Mekelle on October 3, 2026, following the TPLF's withdrawal. While the mood in Addis Ababa is celebratory, the situation remains complex. The war's roots lie in unresolved political grievances, with multiple authorities claiming governance over Tigray. The federal government faces challenges in establishing legitimacy and authority, as many Tigrayans view the TPLF as their representative. The humanitarian crisis in the region is dire, with millions needing assistance. The future stability of Ethiopia hinges on whether the federal government can gain the consent of Tigrayans and address the underlying sociopolitical issues rather than merely exert military control.

somalia.title: NSA seeks full CAF approval for Essipong Stadium ahead of Ghana-Somalia fixture - 3News
somalia.summary: The National Sports Authority (NSA) is seeking full approval from the Confederation of African Football (CAF) for the Essipong Stadium in Sekondi-Takoradi ahead of the upcoming international fixture between Ghana and Somalia. The stadium, which has undergone renovations, is being evaluated to ensure it meets CAF's standards for hosting international matches. The NSA is working diligently to address any outstanding issues to secure the necessary certification. This approval is crucial for the match scheduled to take place as part of the qualifiers for the Africa Cup of Nations. The NSA is optimistic about meeting the requirements in time for the fixture.

somalia.title: More than 20 children from Somalia feared trafficked to Ireland - Irish Examiner
somalia.summary: More than 20 children from Somalia are feared to have been trafficked to Ireland, according to reports. The children, some as young as 12, are believed to have arrived in the country unaccompanied and are at significant risk of exploitation. Authorities are concerned about their safety and well-being, as the children may be vulnerable to various forms of abuse. The Irish government and relevant agencies are working to investigate the situation and provide support to the affected children. This alarming situation highlights ongoing issues related to human trafficking and the need for enhanced protective measures for vulnerable minors.

somalia.title: SLAUGHTERED CIVILIANS?: Questions surround Ilhan Omar’s father’s alleged actions in Somalia - News24
somalia.summary: Ilhan Omar's father's past actions during the Somali Civil War have come under scrutiny, raising questions about his involvement in the conflict. Reports suggest that he may have been linked to a militia responsible for violence against civilians. Omar has previously described her father's role as a humanitarian, but critics argue that his actions could contradict this narrative. The allegations have sparked a debate about the complexities of the civil war and the responsibilities of those involved. Omar has not directly addressed the claims but continues to focus on her political work and advocacy. The situation highlights the challenges of reconciling personal history with public perception in a politically charged environment.

somalia.title: US Airstrikes in Somalia Face Civilian Harm Scrutiny - https://kulu-media.com/
somalia.summary: US airstrikes in Somalia are under scrutiny due to concerns about civilian casualties. Recent reports indicate that these military operations, aimed at targeting militant groups, have resulted in unintended harm to non-combatants. Human rights organizations and local advocates are calling for greater transparency and accountability regarding the impact of these strikes on civilian populations. Critics argue that the lack of precise intelligence and oversight can lead to tragic outcomes, emphasizing the need for a reassessment of military strategies in the region. The US military maintains that it takes precautions to minimize civilian harm, but the ongoing debate highlights the complexities of conducting counterterrorism operations in populated areas.

somalia.title: US Raises Kenya Travel Advisory to Level 3: What It Means for Somalia - FTL Somalia
somalia.summary: The U.S. State Department has elevated its travel advisory for Kenya to Level 3, urging travelers to reconsider their trips due to increased risks, particularly related to terrorism and crime. This advisory reflects concerns about potential threats from extremist groups, including Al-Shabaab, which operates in neighboring Somalia. The advisory highlights the dangers of traveling to certain areas in Kenya, especially near the Somali border. As a result, the advisory may impact travel plans for those considering visits to Somalia, as it underscores the regional security challenges. Travelers are advised to stay informed about the situation and take necessary precautions if they choose to proceed with their plans.

somalia.title: Somalia warns media outlets over alleged terrorist propaganda - Shabelle Media Network
somalia.summary: Somalia's government has issued a warning to media outlets regarding the dissemination of content that could be perceived as terrorist propaganda. Authorities are concerned that certain reports may inadvertently support or glorify extremist groups, particularly Al-Shabaab. The government emphasized the importance of responsible journalism and urged media organizations to adhere to ethical standards when reporting on security issues. Officials highlighted the potential consequences of spreading such narratives, which could undermine national security efforts. The warning reflects ongoing challenges in combating terrorism and the role of media in shaping public perception. The government is calling for collaboration with media entities to ensure accurate and constructive reporting.

somalia.title: Somalia steps up El Niño preparedness with UN, Norway support - Shabelle Media Network
somalia.summary: Somalia is enhancing its preparedness for the El Niño phenomenon with support from the United Nations and Norway. The country is taking proactive measures to mitigate the potential impacts of the climate event, which is expected to bring heavy rainfall and could lead to flooding and other challenges. The collaboration aims to strengthen Somalia's resilience against climate-related disasters, ensuring that communities are better equipped to handle the adverse effects. Authorities are focusing on improving early warning systems and response strategies to safeguard vulnerable populations. This initiative highlights the importance of international cooperation in addressing climate change and its repercussions on food security and livelihoods in Somalia.

somalia.title: Somalia, Spain agree to explore formal political consultations - Shabelle Media Network
somalia.summary: Somalia and Spain have agreed to initiate formal political consultations to strengthen their bilateral relations. The agreement was reached during a meeting between Somali Foreign Minister Abshir Omar Jama and Spanish Ambassador to Somalia, José Antonio Sainz. Both parties expressed their commitment to enhancing cooperation in various sectors, including security, trade, and development. The discussions also aimed to address mutual interests and challenges faced by both nations. This initiative marks a significant step in fostering diplomatic ties and collaboration between Somalia and Spain, reflecting a shared desire for stability and progress in the region.

somalia.title: AJF × SDRB Somalia Business Plan Competition 2026 - Opportunity Desk
somalia.summary: The AJF × SDRB Somalia Business Plan Competition 2026 is an initiative aimed at fostering entrepreneurship in Somalia. The competition invites aspiring entrepreneurs to submit innovative business plans that address local challenges and contribute to economic development. Participants will have the opportunity to receive mentorship, training, and funding to help bring their ideas to fruition. The competition emphasizes the importance of sustainable and impactful business solutions. Interested individuals can apply through the official website, with the deadline for submissions set for early 2026. This initiative is part of a broader effort to support the growth of the Somali economy and empower the next generation of business leaders in the region.

somalia.title: Somalia, Morocco Boost Energy and Mining Cooperation - Somali National News Agency
somalia.summary: Somalia and Morocco have agreed to enhance cooperation in the energy and mining sectors. The agreement was reached during a meeting between Somali Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources, Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, and Moroccan Minister of Energy Transition and Sustainable Development, Leila Benali. Both nations aim to share expertise and resources to develop their energy and mining industries. The collaboration is expected to facilitate investment opportunities and promote sustainable practices in these sectors. This partnership reflects a growing trend of African nations working together to leverage their natural resources for economic development.

football.title: حرب تصريحات.. الهلال السوداني يرد على رئيس اتحاد الكرة! - winwin
football.summary: الهلال السوداني رد على تصريحات رئيس اتحاد الكرة السوداني، الذي انتقد أداء الفريق في الدوري. جاء الرد من إدارة الهلال عبر بيان رسمي، حيث أكدت أن الانتقادات غير مبررة وأن الفريق يسعى لتحقيق النجاح رغم التحديات. كما أشار الهلال إلى التزامه بتطوير كرة القدم في السودان ودعم اللاعبين. البيان شدد على أهمية التعاون بين الأندية والاتحاد لتحقيق الأهداف المشتركة، ودعا إلى التركيز على تحسين الأداء بدلاً من الانشغال بالتصريحات. هذه الحرب الكلامية تعكس التوترات الحالية في الساحة الرياضية السودانية، حيث يسعى كل طرف لتأكيد موقفه.

football.title: الهلال السوداني يصنع الحدث و"غربال" على موعد مع المجد - شبكة تواصل الإخبارية
football.summary: الهلال السوداني حقق إنجازًا كبيرًا في مسيرته الكروية، حيث تمكن من الوصول إلى مراحل متقدمة في المنافسات القارية. اللاعب "غربال" كان له دور بارز في هذا النجاح، حيث أظهر مهاراته العالية وأداءه المتميز في المباريات. الجماهير تتطلع إلى المزيد من الإنجازات، مع آمال كبيرة في تحقيق الألقاب. الهلال يسعى لتعزيز مكانته في الساحة الرياضية، ويبدو أن الفريق في طريقه لتحقيق المجد الذي يطمح إليه.

football.title: الهلال السوداني والسويحلي الليبي يقتربان من مجموعات دوري الأبطال - مانكيش نت
football.summary: اقترب فريق الهلال السوداني وفريق السويحلي الليبي من التأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا. جاء ذلك بعد الأداء القوي الذي قدمه الفريقان في المباريات التمهيدية. الهلال السوداني حقق نتائج إيجابية في مبارياته السابقة، مما يعزز فرصه في التأهل، بينما تمكن السويحلي من تقديم عرض قوي في التصفيات. يتطلع كلا الفريقين إلى تحقيق النجاح في المرحلة المقبلة من البطولة، حيث تعتبر هذه المنافسة فرصة كبيرة لإظهار مهاراتهم على المستوى القاري.

football.title: الهلال السوداني والسويحلي الليبي يقتربان من دور المجموعات في دوري ابطال افريقيا - Elsport
football.summary: اقترب فريق الهلال السوداني وفريق السويحلي الليبي من التأهل إلى دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بعد أدائهما القوي في التصفيات. حيث حقق الهلال السوداني فوزاً مهماً على منافسه في مباراة الذهاب، مما يعزز فرصه في التأهل. من جهة أخرى، قدم السويحلي الليبي عرضاً مميزاً في مباراته، مما يضعه في موقف جيد للتقدم في البطولة. يتطلع كلا الفريقين إلى تحقيق نتائج إيجابية في مباريات الإياب لضمان مكانهما في دور المجموعات، حيث تعتبر هذه المرحلة من البطولة ذات أهمية كبيرة للأندية الأفريقية.

football.title: الهلال السوداني يحسم مواجهة سيداما بونا ويقترب من التأهل الأفريقي - اخبار السودان
football.summary: حقق فريق الهلال السوداني فوزًا مهمًا على سيداما بونا الإثيوبي في مباراة ضمن تصفيات دوري أبطال أفريقيا، مما يقربه من التأهل للمرحلة التالية. انتهت المباراة بفوز الهلال بنتيجة 2-0، حيث سجل الأهداف كل من اللاعب محمد عبد الرحمن واللاعب وليد الشعلة. قدم الفريق أداءً قويًا خلال المباراة، مما ساهم في تعزيز فرصه في المنافسة على اللقب الأفريقي. بهذا الفوز، يواصل الهلال مسيرته الناجحة في البطولة ويعزز من موقفه في المجموعة.

football.title: موعد بث مواجهة الهلال وسيداما والقنوات الناقلة للقاء المرتقب اليوم - موقع رادار
football.summary: تقام اليوم مواجهة مرتقبة بين فريق الهلال وسيداما، حيث ينتظر عشاق كرة القدم هذه المباراة بفارغ الصبر. ستبدأ المباراة في تمام الساعة 8:00 مساءً بتوقيت مكة المكرمة. سيتم بث اللقاء عبر عدة قنوات، منها القناة الرياضية السعودية، بالإضافة إلى منصات البث المباشر على الإنترنت. يُعتبر هذا اللقاء مهمًا للفريقين، حيث يسعى الهلال لتحقيق الفوز لتعزيز موقفه في البطولة، بينما يأمل سيداما في تقديم أداء قوي أمام خصمهم.

football.title: موعد مباراة الهلال السوداني وسيداما كوفي | مبتدا - مبتدا
football.summary: تقام مباراة الهلال السوداني وسيداما كوفي في إطار منافسات دوري أبطال أفريقيا. يُنتظر أن تُعقد المباراة في يوم 15 أكتوبر 2023، حيث يسعى الهلال السوداني لتحقيق الفوز على الفريق الإثيوبي. يُعتبر الهلال من الأندية العريقة في السودان، ويأمل في تقديم أداء قوي أمام سيداما كوفي لتعزيز فرصه في البطولة. المباراة ستُقام على ملعب الهلال في الخرطوم، مما يمنح الفريق ميزة اللعب على أرضه وأمام جماهيره.
